name: Claude Code workflow fan-out prefix staggering (CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS)
reasoning:
What the model reads is untouched: every staggered sibling agent still sends the byte-identical shared prompt prefix. The only thing that changes is *when* each sibling's first request is dispatched — later agents are delayed just long enough that their request arrives after the first sibling's cache write has landed server-side, so they read a cache entry instead of racing to create their own (each of which would otherwise pay full or cache-write price for an identical prefix). Quote, verified verbatim against the raw changelog: 'Improved workflow fan-outs to stagger same-prefix sibling agents so subsequent agents read the cached prompt prefix instead of re-paying it (`CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS=0` disables)' — found at line 161 of CHANGELOG.md under the '## 2.1.229' heading, exactly as claimed. This stops holding the moment `CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS=0` is set (the race the feature exists to avoid returns), or when the fixed stagger interval is shorter than the server's actual cache-write latency for that prefix length/model (silent race resumption, no error surfaced), or when sibling prompts diverge before the shared-prefix boundary (no common cache key to land on in the first place).

On challenge: both refuters overturned this. The verifiable facts — the env var, the changelog line — hold, but the mechanism narrative doing the argumentative work was uncited and, checked against the primary source, wrong in its specifics. The category is plausibly right; the submission is not sound as sourced, and this register does not publish a verdict on a narrative nobody could quote.

name: Claude's text watermark (SynthID-style keyed token selection)
reasoning:
Anthropic's own explainer describes an actual change to the generation mechanism, not merely an outcome promise: at points where multiple next-word choices are roughly tied, token selection is driven by a hidden per-response key plus recent context rather than ordinary sampling. Verbatim, checked against the raw article HTML: 'Instead of using an arbitrary random number generator to pick the next word, watermarking uses the key and a few words that come before to settle what word the model should pick.' That is a structural admission that the process choosing output tokens differs from the unwatermarked baseline at qualifying decision points — which is precisely the register's FAIL condition (a different mechanism decides what gets produced), even though the same source separately asserts, also verified verbatim, 'produces no extra tokens, the model is the same price to serve and use' and 'does not impact the quality of Claude's output. To a reader, a watermarked response is indistinguishable from an unwatermarked one.' Those two sentences are the provider's word about the consequence of an admitted mechanism change — they are not evidence that no change occurred, because the change itself is disclosed, not inferred from a promise. This verdict rests on Anthropic's own description of the mechanism, so it would only be revisited if that description were shown to be inaccurate — e.g. if watermarking turned out to apply only after sampling with no effect on which token is chosen, contradicting this very source.

On challenge: the advocate overturned a FAIL, and was right to. The bar is a three-part disjunction — different tokens read, different model answering, different amount of thinking — and a keyed-PRF replacing an RNG at the sampling step trips none of them: same input, same weights, same thinking budget. The FAIL had substituted a broader self-authored test ("a different mechanism decides what gets produced") for the bar's actual text, which is the same paraphrase-as-standard failure the register polices in sources. It rests here rather than higher because the equivalence claim — no quality impact, indistinguishable to a reader — is an assertion this project did not verify, and its supporting measurement is Google DeepMind's on Gemini traffic (SynthID-Text, Nature 2024), not anyone's on Anthropic's deployment.

name: Sidekiq Enterprise Unique Jobs -- default lock key (class, args, queue), computed from the job's own content
reasoning:
Unique Jobs runs inside the customer's own Sidekiq/Redis process -- squarely the 'customer runs the gateway themselves' case this project's scope admits. The lock key is built from the job's own args at push time, so for a job whose args ARE the model request payload, a duplicate push with byte-identical args is refused before it ever reaches Redis, while a push with different args (a genuinely different prompt) gets a different key and is never wrongly deduped -- the exact caller-chosen-label failure mode absent here. Decided by, verified verbatim against the raw HTML of github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Ent-Unique-Jobs on 2026-08-17: 'Jobs are considered unique based on (class, args, queue), meaning a job with the same args can be pushed to different queues.' and, on lock duration, 'The unique_until option allows you to control when the unique lock is removed. The default value is success: the job will not unlock until it executes successfully.' When the lock blocks a push: zero tokens, the duplicate job -- and whatever model call it would have made -- never runs. When it doesn't block: the job that runs is unmodified, same args, same model call as always. Stops holding under conditions Sidekiq discloses rather than hides: the unique_for TTL can expire mid-retry ('If your job retries for a while, 10 minutes can pass, thus allowing another copy of the same job to be pushed to Redis'), and the same page states outright, in bold: 'Design your jobs so that uniqueness is considered best effort, not a 100% guarantee.'

On challenge: both refuters overturned. The default lock key (class, args, queue) is content-derived only if the args ARE the model request, and Sidekiq's own guidance is the opposite — keep args small, pass identifiers, resolve the real request at execution time, because args are serialised into Redis. Under the documented pattern the key is an enqueue-time label, and two enqueues sharing it can resolve to different model requests if the conversation, document or retrieved context moved between pushes. That is the same content-blindness that failed BullMQ at id 189, arrived at from the opposite direction: not a caller-supplied string, but a content-derived key over the wrong content.
savings: No percentage documented (self-hosted, unmetered by any provider). The saving is one duplicate job's entire downstream model call avoided per lock hold, bounded by unique_for/unique_until and explicitly disclaimed by Sidekiq itself as best-effort rather than absolute. Not measured in this sweep.

name: AWS SQS FIFO ContentBasedDeduplication — SHA-256 of message body
reasoning: SQS FIFO, with ContentBasedDeduplication on and no explicit MessageDeduplicationId, computes the dedup ID itself as SHA-256(body) — a key AWS derives from content, not one the caller invents. A second SendMessage with a byte-identical body inside the interval is accepted but only one copy is ever handed to a consumer, so a consumer that calls a model on receipt calls it once per distinct body, not once per enqueue.
